source.title: How Effective Is Constitutional AI in Small LLMs? A Study on DeepSeek-R1 and Its Peers
source.authors: Antonio-Gabriel Chac'on Menke; Tan Xuan Phan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies abliteration, described as removing a single activation direction, and reports its effects on refusal and benchmark performance. It does not report the original difference-in-means extraction procedure or test adding the direction.
record.gate_note: The study reports HarmBench harmful-response rates before and after a prompted constitutional-AI critique-and-revision process. Because that behavior is deliberately elicited by the prompts, those rates do not test whether refusal is mediated by the direction; they are not included as claim-version rows. The paper does state that abliteration appears to remove refusal behavior in Llama-based models, and reports original-versus-abliterated benchmark scores.
record.test_reason: Abliteration (Labonne's weight edit) is mainly a tool here, used to strip pre-existing safety before testing Constitutional AI. The study still reports its own original-versus-abliterated benchmark scores for four released 7-9B models. It also states that abliteration removes refusal in Llama-based models. These results bear on the 'other abilities largely kept' part of V1 and on V2, in a new setting that includes a reasoning model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the paper's main conclusion is about Constitutional AI: self-critique cuts harm most in Llama-based models, especially R1-Llama, whose reasoning is credited. Abliteration side effects are secondary. They are minimal for Llama-based models and larger for Qwen2.5 and Gemma-2. For those two, abliteration seems to disrupt the link between moral understanding and its application, while SafetyBench harm recognition is largely retained.
record.recipe_differences: Uses abliteration, described as removing a single activation direction, but does not state how the direction was extracted or that it was projected out at every layer and position. It does not add the direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Abliteration's benchmark effects vary by model and task. For Gemma-2, prepending system prompts to user prompts led to higher harmful-response scores; the paper otherwise used model-default prompt templates. These prompt findings concern the prompted CAI procedure, not a direct test of the refusal direction.
record.problems: Refusal removal is reported qualitatively, without per-model refusal rates or a stated baseline. The paper does not detail how it obtained the direction or report an addition test. Benchmark results are reported without uncertainty estimates. The CAI response-rate findings are elicited by explicit critique and revision prompts.

untested.parts: The study does not describe how the direction was extracted, gives no refusal rate before or after ablation, and does not test adding the direction to induce refusal.
There are no per-model refusal rates and no pre-abliteration HarmBench baseline. Refusal removal is asserted only for Llama-based models.
Not tested directly. SafetyBench harm recognition largely survives abliteration, but the study does not frame this as harm being encoded separately from refusal.
The study does not examine the direction inside reasoning traces and gives no refusal rate for R1-Llama.

missing.what: SafetyBench scores before and after abliteration for all models. These show capability or harm-recognition costs, e.g. Gemma PhysicalHealth 89.8 to 79.6, Gemma IllegalActivities 88.6 to 81.3, Qwen EthicsMorality 85.4 to 77.4, Llama PhysicalHealth 87.9 to 83.8.

Initial (pre-critique) HarmBench harmful-response rates of the abliterated models. R1-Llama's is 54.4%; the other figure labels (about 45.6%, 76.7% and 87.8%) cannot be matched reliably to the remaining models from the extracted text. These are not elicited by the CAI prompts and indicate how fully refusal was removed. No pre-abliteration baseline is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The study is short and abliteration is a preprocessing tool, so the evidence on the claim is limited to capability-retention tables and one qualitative sentence on refusal removal. The gate note wrongly treats all HarmBench rates as CAI-elicited: the initial-response rates measure the abliterated models directly, though without a baseline. The authors note that the Qwen capability drop matches Arditi et al.'s earlier Qwen observations; that is a cited result, not a row. Arditi et al. is the original source and is not this study.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not specify that its removed direction was extracted as the harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation difference, test projection at every layer and position, or test adding the direction to induce refusal. It does not directly quantify refusal rates before and after ablation.
The paper does not directly report refusal rates for each released model, nor does it establish that refusal removal generalizes beyond the reported Llama-based models.
No jailbreak suppression of the direction or training against its ablation is tested.
No alternative refusal geometry or multiple-direction account is tested.
No separate encoding of harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions is tested.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test is reported.
The study does not vary refusal-training procedures or stages to test whether they determine the existence of a removable direction.
Although R1-Llama is included, the study does not test whether the claimed direction mediates refusal in a reasoning model.

tranche.reason: It uses abliteration mainly as a tool, but it reports its own original-vs-abliterated benchmark results on four 7-9B models (including a reasoning distill) and states that refusal was removed. source_check.notes: The only quantitative signal on refusal removal is Figure 1: initial harmful-response means after abliteration on 90 HarmBench prompts (54.4, 87.8, 45.6, 76.7%). No row records it, the text can't place the means on their panels, and no pre-abliteration baseline or harm judge is given. So every 'refusal removed' verdict rests on the authors' qualitative words. The record's uncertainty=y flag rests only on the CAI harm-reduction SDs; Table 1 tiny-benchmark changes come with no uncertainty.

statements.correction: arXiv:2503.17365 gives no uncertainty for any original-vs-abliterated benchmark value. Its only spread is the SD of CAI harm reduction (±31.60% R1-Llama vs ±49.02% Llama-3.1).
statements.problem: The numbers are right (Llama 3.1-8B MMLU 68.3->68.1, tiny GSM8k 75.0->74.9), and so is 'direction source not stated'. But 'uncertainty y' overstates this study: Table 1's benchmark scores carry no uncertainty.

statements.correction: The prepended prompts were 'You are a helpful AI assistant' (initial/revision) and an 'ethical evaluator' prompt (critique), not a safety system prompt.
statements.problem: Accurate: Gemma-2 (abliterated) gave higher harm scores in initial and revised responses when the system prompt was prepended, and no number is given.

statements.correction: arXiv:2503.17365 only says abliteration (Labonne 2025) removes 'a single activation direction'; the extraction method is not stated. Benchmark values carry no uncertainty. The refusal-removal statement covers the Llama-based models jointly and is qualitative.
statements.problem: The numbers are right (R1-Distill-Llama-8B MMLU 55.7->55.7, tiny GSM8k 65.9->62.9). But the 'what' line names a mean-difference direction, which this study never states, and 'uncertainty' is overstated for these values.
Accurate: the authors only state removal qualitatively and give no refusal rate.
